backward-time-evolution-operator-280a590.title: Quantum Time Evolution Operator in Natural Units
backward-time-evolution-operator-280a590.description: Represents the unitary time-translation operator for quantum states generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian in natural units ($\hbar = 1$). It also serves as the right-hand unitary factor governing observable evolution in the Heisenberg picture.
backward-time-evolution-operator-280a590.conceptual_definition: The exponential operator $e^{-i\hat{H}t}$ is the formal solution to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation $\frac{d}{dt}|\psi(t)\rangle = -i\hat{H}|\psi(t)\rangle$ under a stationary Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ in natural units ($\hbar = 1$). It acts as the unitary propagator $\hat{U}(t) = e^{-i\hat{H}t}$ translating quantum states forward across duration $t$, and features as the adjoint propagator in the Heisenberg transformation $\hat{A}(t) = e^{i\hat{H}t}\hat{A}(0)e^{-i\hat{H}t}$.
backward-time-evolution-operator-280a590.interpretation: The component $\hat{H}$ denotes the self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator acting as the generator of time translations. The parameter $t$ is the elapsed real time parameter. The product $\hat{H}t$ defines the operator-valued dynamical phase, rendered dimensionless by working in natural units where $\hbar = 1$. The imaginary unit $i$ guarantees that the operator is unitary ($e^{-i\hat{H}t}(e^{-i\hat{H}t})^\dagger = \hat{I}$), which preserves total probability and Hilbert-space norm.
backward-time-evolution-operator-280a590.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $t \to 0$, $e^{-i\hat{H}t} \to \hat{I}$, recovering the identity transformation. For infinitesimal duration $\delta t \to 0$, it expands to the first-order form $\hat{I} - i\hat{H}\delta t$. In the stationary limit on an energy eigenstate $\hat{H}|n\rangle = E_n|n\rangle$, the operator evaluates to the dynamical scalar phase factor $e^{-iE_n t}$.
backward-time-evolution-operator-280a590.symmetry_origin: Rooted in continuous time-translation symmetry via Noether's theorem and Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups, establishing the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ as the self-adjoint infinitesimal generator of time translations.

partial-derivative-of-lagrangian-with-re.title: Partial Derivative of Lagrangian with Respect to Generalized Coordinate
partial-derivative-of-lagrangian-with-re.description: Represents the variation of the Lagrangian function with respect to a change in a generalized coordinate, defining the generalized force acting along that degree of freedom.
partial-derivative-of-lagrangian-with-re.conceptual_definition: In analytical mechanics, the partial derivative $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q^i}$ quantifies the rate of change of the Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}(q, \dot{q}, t) = T - V$ with respect to the generalized coordinate $q^i$ while holding generalized velocities $\dot{q}^j$ and time $t$ fixed. In the Euler-Lagrange equation of motion $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}^i}\right) - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q^i} = 0$, this quantity represents the generalized force $Q_i = \dot{p}_i$ conjugate to the coordinate $q^i$.
partial-derivative-of-lagrangian-with-re.interpretation: For a standard conservative system where kinetic energy $T$ depends only on generalized velocities $\dot{q}^i$ and the potential energy $V$ depends only on generalized coordinates $q^i$, this term simplifies to $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q^i} = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial q^i}$, which is precisely the conservative generalized force. If $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q^i} = 0$, the coordinate $q^i$ is defined as cyclic (or ignorable), guaranteeing by Noether's theorem that the conjugate canonical momentum $p_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}^i}$ is a conserved integral of motion.
partial-derivative-of-lagrangian-with-re.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of a velocity-independent potential $V(q)$, $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q^i} \to -\frac{\partial V}{\partial q^i}$. In free-particle flat spacetime where $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m\delta_{jk}\dot{q}^j\dot{q}^k$, $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q^i} = 0$ everywhere, reflecting complete translational homogeneity.
partial-derivative-of-lagrangian-with-re.symmetry_origin: Under continuous spatial translations or rotations of the generalized coordinate $q^i$, invariance of the action (and Lagrangian) implies $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q^i} = 0$, leading directly via Noether's theorem to the conservation of the conjugate momentum $p_i$.

neutrino-mass-right-handed-neutrino-mass.title: Neutrino Mass-Right-Handed Neutrino Mass Seesaw Scale Correspondence
neutrino-mass-right-handed-neutrino-mass.description: Establishes the numerical correspondence between sub-electronvolt active Majorana neutrino masses and intermediate-to-GUT scale right-handed Majorana neutrino masses via the Type-I seesaw mechanism assuming electroweak-scale Dirac masses.
neutrino-mass-right-handed-neutrino-mass.conceptual_definition: Under the standard Type-I seesaw mechanism, the light active neutrino mass scale $m_{\nu}$ is generated via the suppression of an electroweak Dirac mass scale $m_D \sim v = 246\text{ GeV}$ (or $m_D \sim v/\sqrt{2}$) by a heavy gauge-singlet Majorana mass scale $M_R$, yielding the benchmark numerical relation $m_{\nu} \approx 0.1\text{ eV} \iff M_R \approx 10^{14}\text{ GeV}$.
neutrino-mass-right-handed-neutrino-mass.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $M_R \to \infty$, the heavy right-handed states completely decouple from low-energy effective field theory and $m_{\nu} \to 0$. In the limit $M_R \to 0$, the standard seesaw inversion breaks down and the system transitions to a pseudo-Dirac or Dirac neutrino regime.
neutrino-mass-right-handed-neutrino-mass.symmetry_origin: Arises from the spontaneous and explicit breakdown of global total lepton number $B - L$ symmetry at the high energy scale $M_R$ down to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lepton parity, alongside the Standard Model gauge symmetry $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y \to U(1)_{\text{em}}$.

neutrino-mass-right-handed-neutrino-mass.intuitive_summary: Active neutrinos are extraordinarily light not because their underlying Yukawa couplings are unnaturally minuscule, but because their mass is inversely proportional to a superheavy right-handed neutrino mass near the Grand Unification scale.

equation-of-straight-line-motion-in-flat.title: Equation of Straight-Line Motion in Flat Spacetime
equation-of-straight-line-motion-in-flat.description: Governs the unaccelerated worldline of a free particle in flat Minkowski spacetime parameterized by an affine parameter.
equation-of-straight-line-motion-in-flat.conceptual_definition: The equation of straight-line motion in flat spacetime, $\frac{d^2 x^\mu}{d\lambda^2} = 0$, represents the geodesic equation when the affine connection vanishes identically, $\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta} = 0$, in global inertial coordinates. It states that the tangent four-vector $u^\mu = \frac{dx^\mu}{d\lambda}$ is parallel-transported along itself, resulting in a constant coordinate velocity and zero four-acceleration.
equation-of-straight-line-motion-in-flat.interpretation: In this equation, $x^\mu$ denotes the spacetime coordinates $(\mu \in \{0,1,2,3\})$ of the particle's trajectory, and $\lambda$ is an affine parameter along the worldline (such as proper time $\tau$ for timelike trajectories or an affine parameter for null rays). The second derivative $\frac{d^2 x^\mu}{d\lambda^2}$ represents the coordinate four-acceleration. Setting this term to zero demonstrates that inertial trajectories are straight lines in Minkowski spacetime with constant tangent vectors $\frac{dx^\mu}{d\lambda}$.
equation-of-straight-line-motion-in-flat.limits_and_boundary: Valid strictly in flat spacetime or locally in a Local Inertial Frame (LIF) where the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}$ vanish. In curved spacetime, tidal forces emerge and the full geodesic equation $\frac{d^2 x^\mu}{d\lambda^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta} \frac{dx^\alpha}{d\lambda} \frac{dx^\beta}{d\lambda} = 0$ must be used.
equation-of-straight-line-motion-in-flat.symmetry_origin: Poincaré invariance (spacetime translation and Lorentz invariance) of Minkowski spacetime, which implies the conservation of the four-momentum vector $p^\mu = m \frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}$ via Noether's theorem.

non-zero-scalar-field-vacuum-expectation.title: Non-Zero Scalar Field Vacuum Expectation Value (Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking)
non-zero-scalar-field-vacuum-expectation.description: States that the ground-state expectation value of a quantum scalar field operator is non-vanishing, establishing the order parameter for spontaneous symmetry breaking.
non-zero-scalar-field-vacuum-expectation.conceptual_definition: In quantum field theory, the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of a scalar field $\phi(x)$ characterizes the lowest energy state $|0\rangle$ of the system. When the potential possesses degenerate minima away from the field origin, the true vacuum spontaneously chooses a specific minimum, resulting in a non-zero expectation value $\langle 0 | \phi | 0 \rangle = v \neq 0$. This non-zero background condensate breaks the global or gauge symmetries of the Lagrangian down to the stabilizer subgroup of the vacuum state.
non-zero-scalar-field-vacuum-expectation.interpretation: The state vector $|0\rangle$ denotes the Lorentz-invariant quantum vacuum ground state. The operator $\phi$ is the scalar field operator acting on Fock space. The quantity $v$ is the classical background value (VEV) with mass dimension $[M]^1$ in four-dimensional spacetime. Because $v \neq 0$, field fluctuations are canonically redefined as $\phi(x) = v + h(x)$, where $\langle 0 | h(x) | 0 \rangle = 0$, revealing physical particle excitations $h(x)$ and generating mass terms via Yukawa and gauge couplings.
non-zero-scalar-field-vacuum-expectation.limits_and_boundary: In the high-temperature limit $T > T_c$ (symmetry restoration), thermal fluctuations restore the symmetric phase such that $\langle \phi \rangle_T \to 0$. In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the VEV $v$ corresponds to the absolute minimum of the classical potential $V(\phi)$.
non-zero-scalar-field-vacuum-expectation.symmetry_origin: Originates in spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) of continuous global or local gauge symmetries (e.g., $U(1)$, $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$), where the Lagrangian remains invariant under symmetry transformations while the vacuum state $|0\rangle$ is non-invariant.

inverse-delta-factor-cb051420.description: Represents the multiplicative inverse of a characteristic scale, finite difference, detuning, or spectral gap parameter $\Delta$.
inverse-delta-factor-cb051420.conceptual_definition: The inverse delta factor, denoted $\frac{1}{\Delta}$, is the algebraic reciprocal of a characteristic physical parameter $\Delta$ (such as an energy detuning, finite difference, or band gap). inverse-delta-factor-cb051420.interpretation: The symbol $\Delta$ represents a characteristic parameter scale, such as an energy detuning $\Delta = \omega - \omega_0$, spatial discretization interval $\Delta x$, or spectral gap. The reciprocal $\frac{1}{\Delta}$ sets the characteristic response time, inverse correlation length, or effective coupling strength in adiabatic elimination and perturbation expansions.
inverse-delta-factor-cb051420.limits_and_boundary: In the large-scale limit $\Delta \to \infty$, the factor $\frac{1}{\Delta} \to 0$, corresponding to complete decoupling. In the resonance or zero-gap limit $\Delta \to 0$, $\frac{1}{\Delta} \to \pm \infty$, marking the breakdown of perturbative regimes and the onset of strong coupling.
inverse-delta-factor-cb051420.symmetry_origin: Scale covariance under algebraic inversion, mapping dilatation transformations $\Delta \to \lambda \Delta$ into reciprocal scaling factors $\frac{1}{\Delta} \to \lambda^{-1} \frac{1}{\Delta}$.

differential-stellar-mass-distribution-4.title: Differential Stellar Initial Mass Distribution
differential-stellar-mass-distribution-4.description: Represents the differential number of stars formed per unit volume (or per star-forming event) within an infinitesimal stellar mass interval.
differential-stellar-mass-distribution-4.conceptual_definition: The differential stellar mass distribution $dN = \xi(M) dM$ defines the fundamental measure of the Initial Mass Function (IMF). It quantifies the expected number density of stars born with masses in the infinitesimal interval $[M, M + dM]$, serving as the continuous distribution function from which cumulative stellar counts and total integrated mass in stellar populations are derived.
differential-stellar-mass-distribution-4.interpretation: The term $\xi(M)$ represents the initial mass function (number density of stars per unit mass interval), and $dM$ is the differential element of initial stellar mass. The product $\xi(M) dM$ yields the differential number of stars $dN$. Integrating $\xi(M) dM$ over a mass interval $[M_1, M_2]$ gives the total number of stars $N$, while integrating $M \xi(M) dM$ yields the total stellar mass $M_{\text{tot}}$ formed in that mass regime.
differential-stellar-mass-distribution-4.limits_and_boundary: As $M \to M_{\text{lower}} \approx 0.08\,M_{\odot}$ (the hydrogen-burning limit), $\xi(M)$ flattens or turns over, avoiding a divergence in total mass. As $M \to M_{\text{upper}} \approx 150\text{--}300\,M_{\odot}$ (the Eddington radiation pressure limit), $\xi(M) \to 0$.
differential-stellar-mass-distribution-4.symmetry_origin: Statistical scale-invariance in supersonic turbulent fragmentation and gravitational collapse of interstellar molecular clouds.

motional-electromotive-force-line-integr.title: Motional Electromotive Force Line Integral
motional-electromotive-force-line-integr.description: Represents the closed contour line integral governing the motional flux variation and induced electromotive force in a moving or deforming boundary within a magnetic field.
motional-electromotive-force-line-integr.conceptual_definition: The motional line integral $\oint (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot d\mathbf{l}$ emerges from the kinematic boundary terms of the Leibniz integral rule applied to the magnetic flux $\Phi_B = \iint_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{a}$. When a closed circuit boundary $\mathcal{C}$ moves with velocity $\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r}, t)$, the surface element swept out in time $dt$ along the perimeter $d\mathbf{l}$ is $d\mathbf{a}_{sweep} = (\mathbf{v} dt) \times d\mathbf{l}$. Using vector triple product identities, the rate of flux swept across the boundary corresponds directly to $-\oint (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \oint (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot d\mathbf{l}$.
motional-electromotive-force-line-integr.interpretation: In this expression, $\mathbf{B}$ denotes the magnetic flux density, $\mathbf{v}$ represents the local velocity of the moving circuit element, and $d\mathbf{l}$ is the differential line element directed along the closed curve $\mathcal{C}$. The vector cross product $\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{v}$ defines the convective flux displacement vector per unit time, whose inner product with $d\mathbf{l}$ measures the rate at which magnetic field lines are cut by that segment. The closed line integral $\oint$ sums these convective contributions over the entire loop to yield the total motional rate of change of magnetic flux in units of volts ($V$).
motional-electromotive-force-line-integr.limits_and_boundary: In the stationary limit $\mathbf{v} \to \mathbf{0}$, the integral vanishes identically, reducing induction solely to local temporal variations $\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$. For uniform translation in a homogeneous magnetic field, the integral is zero for closed rigid loops because equal and opposite fluxes enter and exit opposing boundary segments. In the relativistic limit $v \to c$, the non-relativistic cross product $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$ must be replaced by the fully relativistic Lorentz force formulation incorporating the Lorentz factor $\gamma$.
motional-electromotive-force-line-integr.symmetry_origin: Rooted in Galilean relativity of classical electrodynamics and the Lorentz transformation of electromagnetic field tensors $F^{\mu\nu}$ in the low-velocity limit ($v \ll c$), reflecting geometric invariance under continuous deforming path diffeomorphisms.

vector-orthogonality-condition-19525769.title: Vector Orthogonality Condition
vector-orthogonality-condition-19525769.description: This equation states that the dot product of two non-zero vectors is zero if and only if the vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) to each other.
vector-orthogonality-condition-19525769.conceptual_definition: In a real inner product space, the dot product (or scalar product) is a fundamental operation that takes two vectors and returns a scalar. Geometrically, the dot product is related to the cosine of the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are defined as orthogonal if the angle between them is 90 degrees. The equation $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}$ = 0 $\iff \mathbf{A} \perp \mathbf{B}$ provides an algebraic test for this geometric condition.
vector-orthogonality-condition-19525769.interpretation: This formula is a cornerstone of vector algebra and geometry, providing a direct algebraic method to determine if two vectors are perpendicular. It is widely used in physics to analyze situations where components are independent or act at right angles, such as in work-energy theorems (where force perpendicular to displacement does no work) or in defining basis vectors in coordinate systems. It signifies a lack of projection of one vector onto the other.
vector-orthogonality-condition-19525769.limits_and_boundary: This relationship holds true for vectors in any real inner product space, typically $\mathbb{R}^n$. It assumes that neither vector $\mathbf{A}$ nor $\mathbf{B}$ is the zero vector; if either is the zero vector, their dot product is zero, but orthogonality is not uniquely defined in the same geometric sense (though the zero vector is often considered orthogonal to all vectors by convention).
vector-orthogonality-condition-19525769.symmetry_origin: This relationship is a direct consequence of the definition of the dot product and the geometric definition of orthogonality. It does not arise from a specific physical symmetry or conservation law but rather from the inherent algebraic and geometric structure of Euclidean vector spaces.

commuting-operators-condition-dd1717e3.title: Commuting Operators Condition in Quantum Mechanics
commuting-operators-condition-dd1717e3.description: Specifies the condition under which the Lie bracket or commutator of two linear operators vanishes, implying operator commutativity and the existence of a shared basis of eigenstates.
commuting-operators-condition-dd1717e3.conceptual_definition: In quantum mechanics and functional analysis on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, two linear operators $\hat{O}_1$ and $\hat{O}_2$ are defined to commute if their commutator vanishes identically: $[\hat{O}_1, \hat{O}_2] \equiv \hat{O}_1 \hat{O}_2 - \hat{O}_2 \hat{O}_1 = 0$. For self-adjoint operators (observables), this algebraic condition guarantees that the observables are simultaneously measurable without quantum back-action or uncertainty bounds.
commuting-operators-condition-dd1717e3.interpretation: The condition $[\hat{O}_1, \hat{O}_2] = 0$ holds where $[\cdot, \cdot]$ denotes the commutator bracket on the algebra of operators. The operator $\hat{O}_1$ acts first on a state vector followed by $\hat{O}_2$, yielding an identical outcome to the reverse composition $\hat{O}_2 \hat{O}_1$. Physically, by the spectral theorem, commuting self-adjoint operators admit a complete orthonormal basis of simultaneous eigenstates $|n, m\rangle$, establishing that their generalized Heisenberg uncertainty relation satisfies $\sigma_{O_1} \sigma_{O_2} \ge \frac{1}{2} |\langle [\hat{O}_1, \hat{O}_2] \rangle| = 0$. When one operator is the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$, commutativity implies that the other observable corresponds to a continuous symmetry and a conserved quantity.
commuting-operators-condition-dd1717e3.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit where Planck's constant $\hbar \to 0$, quantum commutators map to classical Poisson brackets via Dirac canonical quantization: $\frac{1}{i\hbar} [\hat{O}_1, \hat{O}_2] \to \{O_1, O_2\}_{\text{PB}} = 0$.
commuting-operators-condition-dd1717e3.symmetry_origin: Abelian subalgebras and continuous Lie group symmetries; commuting observables correspond to mutually compatible generators of symmetry transformations.

general-lagrangian-function.title: General Lagrangian Function
general-lagrangian-function.conceptual_definition: In the calculus of variations and analytical mechanics, the Lagrangian $L(f(x), f'(x), x)$ serves as the integrand of the action functional $S[f] = \int L(f(x), f'(x), x) \, dx$. The path $f(x)$ physically realized by the system extremizes $S[f]$ under fixed boundary conditions, yielding the Euler-Lagrange stationary condition $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial f'}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial f} = 0$.
general-lagrangian-function.intuitive_summary: The Lagrangian encodes the instantaneous balance of dynamics and constraints for a system as a function of configuration, rate of change, and independent parameter.
general-lagrangian-function.interpretation: The symbol $L$ denotes the Lagrangian value. The argument $f(x)$ is the state or generalized coordinate at parameter value $x$. The term $f'(x) = \frac{df}{dx}$ denotes the generalized velocity or derivative with respect to $x$. The explicit dependence on $x$ accounts for non-autonomous systems, external driving, or explicit spatial inhomogeneity.
general-lagrangian-function.symmetry_origin: By Noether's first theorem, invariance of $L$ under continuous coordinate transformations $\delta f$ generates conserved generalized momenta $p = \frac{\partial L}{\partial f'}$, while invariance under translations in $x$ leads to conservation of the Jacobi energy function $E_L = f' \frac{\partial L}{\partial f'} - L$.
general-lagrangian-function.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where $x$ represents time $t$ and velocities are non-relativistic ($v \ll c$), $L$ decomposes into kinetic minus potential energy $L = T - V$. When generalized to continuous spatial dimensions, $L$ becomes the spatial integral of a Lagrangian density $\mathcal{L}$.

secular-equation-for-a-single-plane-wave.title: Secular Equation for a Single Plane Wave Component of a Bloch State
secular-equation-for-a-single-plane-wave.conceptual_definition: In solid-state electronic structure theory, expanding a Bloch state $\psi_{\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{\mathbf{G}} C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} e^{i(\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}$ into plane waves transforms the stationary Schrödinger equation into the central matrix eigenvalue problem $\sum_{\mathbf{G}'} H_{\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}'} C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}'} = E C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}}$. When coupling via non-zero reciprocal lattice Fourier components $V_{\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}'}$ is absent or treated in the nearly-free electron diagonal limit, the system decouples into single-component secular equations of the form $(\lambda_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} - E) C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} = 0$, requiring $E = \lambda_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}}$ for non-trivial wave amplitudes.
secular-equation-for-a-single-plane-wave.intuitive_summary: Without the periodic crystal lattice scattering electrons into different Bragg planes, each plane wave propagates independently, with its energy eigenvalue directly matching its diagonal kinetic plus mean potential energy.
secular-equation-for-a-single-plane-wave.interpretation: The parameter $\lambda_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}} = \frac{\hbar^2 |\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}|^2}{2m} + V_0$ represents the unperturbed diagonal energy of a plane-wave state with crystal momentum $\mathbf{k}$ shifted by the reciprocal lattice vector $\mathbf{G}$. The scalar $E$ denotes the energy eigenvalue of the electron state, and $C_{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}}$ is the expansion coefficient (amplitude) of the specific plane-wave component $e^{i(\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}$.
secular-equation-for-a-single-plane-wave.symmetry_origin: Discrete spatial translation symmetry of the Bravais lattice $\mathbf{R}$ according to Bloch's theorem, preserving quasi-momentum $\hbar\mathbf{k}$ modulo reciprocal lattice vectors $\hbar\mathbf{G}$.
secular-equation-for-a-single-plane-wave.limits_and_boundary: In the free-electron limit ($V(\mathbf{r}) \to 0$), the off-diagonal periodic potential terms vanish exactly, yielding the free-electron parabolic band dispersion $E = \frac{\hbar^2 |\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}|^2}{2m}$. Near the Brillouin zone boundary where $|\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}| \approx |\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}'|$, the uncoupled single-component approximation breaks down and degenerate perturbation theory must be applied.
